summary: Jacob’s household is named again as Israel multiplies in Egypt after Joseph’s death. A new king treats that growth as a threat, imposes harsh labor, orders the Hebrew midwives to kill boys at birth, and finally commands his whole people to throw newborn sons into the Nile.
whyItMatters: The book opens with a people whose growth fulfills an ancestral hope but exposes them to organized violence. Shiphrah and Puah’s refusal is the first narrated resistance to Pharaoh’s program.

context.author: Exodus names no writer of the finished book, though it depicts Moses writing particular words. Later tradition ascribes the Torah to him; its composition remains debated.
context.audience: Israel is addressed through its story of rescue, covenant, and worship; this chapter names no narrower first audience.
context.date: The book gives a relative story sequence but no secure external year for the events. The dating and formation of its finished text remain debated.
context.setting: Egypt after Joseph’s generation, especially forced labor at Pithom and Raamses and the setting of Hebrew births.
context.literaryForm: Opening genealogy and compressed account of escalating royal oppression, answered by the midwives’ refusal.

before.text: Genesis closes with Joseph’s death in Egypt and a promise of a future departure. Exodus names Jacob’s arriving family, then reports Joseph’s generation gone and a new king rising.

here.text: Israel’s growth meets three escalating responses: forced labor, an order to midwives, and a public decree about the Nile.

after.text: The next chapter follows one threatened boy whose family hides him and whose rescue comes through the river named in Pharaoh’s decree.

outline.heading: A family becomes a numerous people
outline.note: Jacob’s descendants are named, Joseph’s generation dies, and Israel multiplies.

outline.heading: Fear and forced labor
outline.note: A new king frames Israel as a danger and burdens them with ruthless work.

outline.heading: The midwives defy an order to kill
outline.note: Shiphrah and Puah preserve boys’ lives and answer Pharaoh’s challenge.

outline.heading: Growth and a wider death decree
outline.note: God deals well with the midwives while Pharaoh orders all his people to cast sons into the river.

keyVerses.text: The children of Israel were fruitful, and increased abundantly, and multiplied, and grew exceedingly mighty; and the land was filled with them.
keyVerses.why: The verse turns the named family into a growing people, setting up Pharaoh’s fear.

keyVerses.text: But the midwives feared God, and didn’t do what the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the baby boys alive.
keyVerses.why: The midwives’ refusal directly opposes the king’s order to kill newborn boys.

keyVerses.text: Pharaoh commanded all his people, saying, “You shall cast every son who is born into the river, and every daughter you shall save alive.”
keyVerses.why: The final order expands violence from the birth stool to the entire population and the Nile.

themes: fear of God versus royal command

questions.question: How does this opening connect the family of Genesis to Israel in Egypt?
questions.answer: It names Jacob’s sons and counts seventy descendants, then records Joseph’s generation dying and the children of Israel multiplying. The story moves from one family’s arrival to a large people living under a new ruler.

questions.question: Does Exodus identify the new king or date his reign?
questions.answer: No. It says a new king arose who did not know Joseph and reports what he feared and did, but it supplies neither his personal name nor a calendar date. Naming a particular pharaoh would require evidence outside this chapter.

questions.question: What are “taskmasters” in this account?
questions.answer: They are officials placed over the Israelites to afflict them with burdens. Their appointment leads into the building of storage cities and the description of bitter work in bricks, mortar, and fields.

questions.question: Does Israel’s growth justify Pharaoh’s fears or his policy?
questions.answer: Pharaoh imagines a future war in which Israel might join an enemy and leave Egypt. The text gives this as his reasoning; it does not report an Israelite attack that warrants forced labor or killing children.

questions.question: What changes when harsh labor fails to reduce the people?
questions.answer: The narrator says oppression is followed by further multiplication and Egyptian dread. Pharaoh then moves from exploiting labor to instructing midwives to kill boys during delivery.

questions.question: What should be made of the midwives’ answer to Pharaoh?
questions.answer: The midwives tell him Hebrew women give birth before they arrive, while the narrator has already said the women deliberately disobeyed because they feared God. The passage praises their life-preserving refusal without independently verifying every detail of their explanation.

questions.question: Why name Shiphrah and Puah while leaving the king unnamed?
questions.answer: The story identifies the two midwives by name and records their refusal and God’s good treatment of them. Pharaoh is known here by title and orders, keeping attention on what these women do when commanded to kill.

questions.question: How broad is the final decree?
questions.answer: Pharaoh commands all his people to cast every newborn son into the river while letting daughters live. This is a wider public order than the earlier instruction to two midwives, and the next chapter begins under its danger.

glossary.def: Officials set over the Israelites to impose burdens in Pharaoh’s forced-labor program.
The place or implement at delivery where Pharaoh expects the midwives to identify and kill sons.
Pithom and Raamses, the cities the Israelites are made to build for Pharaoh.
